They cover parts 1 and 3 only in part. Part 2 has no sources from the denominations' own sites. Verses I couldn't source are left out.

**Missing entirely:**

- A real traditions section. What I can offer instead is a short list of points where the older commentators disagree, after the verse notes.

---

**Whole chapter**
- Enduring Word (David Guzik) says chapter 20 sets the penalties for the laws already given in chapter 18. Chapter 18 speaks to the would-be offender; chapter 20 speaks to the community responsible for enforcing the law (quoting Mark Rooker). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- Matthew Henry: the penalties were added so that people not held back by the fear of God would be held back by fear of punishment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_020.cfm
- Expositor's Bible (Kellogg):
  - This is the criminal law of a nation whose only King was God.
  - The penalties match how wicked each crime is, and are meant to punish rather than to reform the offender.
  - They also aim at the moral cleansing of the whole people.
  - No torture was involved, and the law applied equally to men and women.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/20.htm
- Precept Austin: the death penalty in the Mosaic law covers crimes against God or against the family, not crimes against property or the state. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary

**v. 1:** Ellicott finds the chapter's placement puzzling, since you'd expect it straight after chapter 18. His suggestion is that God first appealed to Israel's high calling in chapter 19, then set civil penalties for those who wouldn't respond to it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm

**v. 2:**
- Enduring Word:
  - Some think children were only passed through fire as a ritual. Guzik allows this may sometimes have happened but says real child sacrifice was certainly part of Molech worship.
  - He says the community did the stoning to show this was a sin against the whole nation.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- Ellicott: "the people of the land" means the whole community, in whose name the judges pass sentence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-20.html
- Matthew Poole (on BibleHub's combined page): "foreigner" covers all residents, not just converts, because these crimes break the law of nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-2.htm
- Gill (same page): more is meant than a ritual of passing through fire; he cites ancient writers on Canaanite child sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-2.htm
- Matthew Henry: Abraham's offering of Isaac can't justify the practice, because God called it off at once. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_020.cfm
- Calvin: children belonged to God through his adoption of Abraham's line, so giving them to idols robbed God and, as far as the parents could, wiped out the grace of adoption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/20.htm
- Modern scholarship (NET notes):
  - The Molech phrase could mean human sacrifice, or dedicating children to some service of Molech, possibly sexual.
  - The Samaritan text (and compare the Septuagint) reads "to cause to serve."
  - https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Lev+18%3A21%3B20%3A2-5

**v. 3:**
- Ellicott:
  - Some read God's "cutting off" as another way of describing the execution itself.
  - Jewish interpreters of the Second Temple period took it to cover cases with too little evidence to convict, where God himself would act.
  - Worshippers "defiled the sanctuary" by coming to worship God after sacrificing their children (Jer. 7; Ezek. 23).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: this doesn't mean the sacrifice was brought into the sanctuary. Rather, all of Israel's sins defiled it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-3.htm

**vv. 4–5:**
- Ellicott: v. 4 covers a community that winks at the crime out of indifference or sympathy. The family is included in v. 5 because they would naturally have known and helped. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Enduring Word: God would prosecute where Israel's courts failed to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- NET notes: the word "spiritual" is added in translation, because the prostitution here is a picture of idolatry, not literal prostitution. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Lev&chapter=20&verse=5

**v. 6:**
- Enduring Word: here God gives Israel no penalty to carry out; he enforces it himself. Occult involvement always separates a person from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- Ellicott: the punishment is the same as for Molech worship, and 1 Chron. 10:13–14 shows it carried out. The mediums themselves were stoned (v. 27). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Precept Austin: consulting a medium was spiritual prostitution, and the person would no longer belong to God's people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary

**vv. 7–8:**
- Ellicott: better translated "ye shall sanctify yourselves," to match Lev. 11:44. Keeping God's laws is how Israel would come to reflect his holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Precept Austin:
  - Holiness isn't achieved by human effort; the name "the LORD who sanctifies you" makes that point.
  - The end of v. 8 joins human responsibility to God's ability.
  - Holiness means a direction of life that makes believers distinct, not moral perfection.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60808/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary

**v. 9:**
- Enduring Word:
  - This is an adult child's settled hostility, probably calling down a death-curse on a parent, not a young child's outburst.
  - Judges rarely if ever carried out the penalty.
  - Jesus quotes this law in Matt. 15:4.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- Calvin: not every insult to a parent carried the death penalty, but the pride that overturns nature was to be hated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/20.htm
- Wenham (cited by Coffman): cursing means more than an angry word; it is the opposite of honouring parents. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-9.html
- Ellicott: later rabbis required death only if the curse used God's own name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-9.htm
- Poole: the verse means bitter abuse or curses, not every bad-tempered word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-9.htm

**v. 10:**
- Enduring Word:
  - The penalty needed two or three eyewitnesses, so it was rarely carried out. Even so, it set out a clear ideal of right and wrong.
  - This helps explain John 8, where the accusers didn't bring the man.
  - Guzik quotes Rooker: the moral law still applies, but these death penalties were limited to Israel as a God-ruled nation.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- Ellicott: Jewish tradition says "shall surely be put to death," with no method named, meant strangling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Expositor's: God ranks adultery alongside murder, not among small sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/20.htm

**vv. 11–12:**
- Calvin: God treats incest as a capital crime against the law of nature (stepmother and stepson; father-in-law and daughter-in-law). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/20.htm
- Enduring Word: chapter 18 left the penalty for incest unstated; here it is death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/

**v. 13:**
- Enduring Word: this is the same penalty as for adultery and incest, applied under the witness rules of Deut. 17:6–7. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
- Gill: both partners are guilty if both consent; the one forced is not (following Aben Ezra). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-13.htm
- Wesley: also excepts a party who was forced (Deut. 22:25). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-13.html
- Matthew Henry: notes that English law of his day also punished these acts with death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_020.cfm

**v. 14:**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this is the only other method of execution named; the offenders were probably stoned first and burned afterwards (Josh. 7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-14.htm
- Poole and Gill: only those who consented were guilty, and an innocent first wife wouldn't die. Gill reports Jewish readings that only one of the women was burned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-14.htm
- Ellicott records the later rabbinic method (molten lead). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-14.htm
- Adam Clarke: the burning was probably branding, not burning alive. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-14.html

**vv. 15–16:** Calvin: God condemns the lust that breaks a boundary even animals keep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/20.htm

**v. 17:**
- Precept Austin: "takes" means sexual relations (the NIV reads "marries"). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60808/
- Calvin: the same punishment applies to brother and sister. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/20.htm

**v. 18:**
- Gill: this isn't about a husband who didn't know. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-18.htm
- BibleHub Study Bible: menstruation made a woman ritually unclean because of blood loss, not because it was morally sinful. https://biblehub.com/study/leviticus/20-18.htm

**vv. 19–21:**
- Precept Austin: these verses don't name death, so the punishment is lighter. Levirate marriage (Deut. 25) is the exception for a brother's widow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary
- Barnes and JFB: "childless" means either that God would deny them children, or that the children would be denied the normal rights of heirs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-21.htm
- Benson: they would have no children, or the children would die first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-20.htm
- Coffman: any children might have been recorded as the dead uncle's or brother's. Gill: since the levirate law has ended, the ban on a brother's wife now has no exceptions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-21.html
- Kretzmann: the marriage wasn't dissolved, but childlessness was a heavy punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/leviticus-20.html
- BibleHub Study Bible: points to John the Baptist rebuking Herod (Mark 6). https://biblehub.com/leviticus/20-21.htm

**vv. 22–23:**
- Ellicott: the chapter ends, as chapter 18 did, with a warning that the land will vomit them out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Precept Austin: "abhorred" carries the sense of disgust. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary
- Pulpit Commentary: because God judged the Canaanites for these acts, these laws are universal moral law, not rules for Israel only. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-13.html

**vv. 24–25:**
- Precept Austin: the same Hebrew word, "separate," is used for God setting Israel apart (v. 24) and Israel distinguishing clean from unclean (v. 25). Acts 10 shows Christ's work has cleansed what was unclean. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary and https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60808/
- Calvin and Ellicott: the food laws were there to keep Israel apart from the nations' pollutions (Dan. 1:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/20.htm, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm

**v. 26:**
- Ellicott: better translated "ye shall be my holy ones." Rabbinic teachers read Israel's separation as a first step, not a rejection of the other nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Enduring Word: God wanted to possess Israel in a relationship, not to force mechanical obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/

**v. 27:**
- Ellicott: women are named because mediums were often women, and because judges might be inclined to spare them. "Their blood is upon them" means they brought death on themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/20.htm
- Precept Austin: inquirers were cut off (v. 6), but practitioners were stoned. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_20_commentary

---

**Where the commentators disagree** (my sources don't tie these to denominations)
- **Do the death penalties still apply?**
  - Rooker (quoted by Enduring Word): no; they were for Israel as a God-ruled nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-20/
  - Kellogg (Expositor's): warns against assuming this law was for Israel only. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/20.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: the forbidden relationships are binding moral law for all nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-13.html
- **What "burned with fire" (v. 14) means:**
  - Clarke: branding.
  - JFB: stoning, then burning the body.
  - Rabbinic tradition (reported by Ellicott and Gill): molten lead.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/20-14.html, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/20-14.htm

To complete the traditions and Catholic/Orthodox sections, the next step would be a new session searching ligonier.org, gty.org, seedbed.com, 1517.org, catholic.com and bibleodyssey.org.
